Incorrect: parameter_server_count also belongs to the tensorflow distribution, for legacy parameter server training. DistributedDataParallel does not use parameter servers.
Correct: process_count_per_instance sets the number of processes on each node and should equal the GPUs per node, so 8 starts one process per GPU.

targets.label: Box 3
why: Incorrect: max_instance_count sets the maximum number of nodes for elastic distributed training. The job needs a fixed four nodes.
Incorrect: shm_size sets the size of the shared memory block of the Docker container, which defaults to 2g. It changes the container, not the number of nodes.
Correct: resources.instance_count is the number of nodes for the job, so 4 runs the training on four nodes of gpu-cluster.

targets.label: Box 4
why: Correct: Learn recommends nccl as the communication backend for GPU-based training because it gives the best performance.
Incorrect: gloo is one of the common torch.distributed backends, but it is not the one that Learn recommends for GPU-based training, where nccl gives the best performance.
Incorrect: mpi is also a common backend, but for GPU-based training Learn recommends nccl for the best performance. The requirement asks for the fastest backend for GPUs.

explanation: A distributed PyTorch command job sets distribution.type to pytorch, process_count_per_instance to the GPUs per node, and resources.instance_count to the number of nodes. Azure Machine Learning starts the processes and sets the environment variables, so the script only calls init_process_group with the env:// method and the nccl backend for GPUs.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. needs to train a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel model on two nodes that have NVIDIA A100 GPUs, with one process per GPU. Training must scale close to linearly, so the nodes need low-latency GPU-to-GPU communication across nodes. An MLClient object named ml_client is connected to the workspace, and no GPU cluster exists yet.

You need to create the compute, submit the job, and follow its output.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `job = command(code="./src", command="python train.py", environment=env, compute="gpu-cluster", instance_count=2, distribution={"type": "PyTorch", "process_count_per_instance": 8})`
`job = command(code="./src", command="python -m torch.distributed.launch --nproc_per_node 8 train.py", environment=env, compute="gpu-cluster")`
explanation: InfiniBand gives low-latency GPU-to-GPU communication across nodes and needs RDMA-capable sizes, usually those with r in the name, such as Standard_ND96asr_v4. You define and create the cluster first, then define a command job whose pytorch distribution starts one process per GPU, and finally submit and stream the job. Learn's example pair, Standard_NC24rs_v3 and Standard_NC24s_v3, follows the same naming rule, but the NCv3 series was retired on September 30, 2025.
rationale: Step 1: Standard_ND96asr_v4 has eight A100 GPUs and InfiniBand, which gives the low-latency cross-node communication that near-linear scaling needs. The cluster definition must exist before you create it.
Step 2: begin_create_or_update() provisions gpu-cluster in the workspace, and result() waits until the operation finishes, so the job can target the cluster.

Step 3: the command job uses two nodes and the pytorch distribution with eight processes per node, one per GPU of Standard_ND96asr_v4, so Azure Machine Learning starts the processes without a launcher.
Step 4: create_or_update() submits the job to gpu-cluster, and stream() follows its logs until the job finishes.

Incorrect: Standard_NC96ads_A100_v4 also has A100 GPUs, four per node, but it has no r in its name and no InfiniBand, so cross-node communication runs over Ethernet and scaling suffers. It suits single-node GPU training.
Incorrect: a launcher utility such as torch.distributed.launch is not needed, and without a distribution and instance_count the job runs on one node only. Use the pytorch distribution instead.

stem:
A distributed PyTorch job at Coho Vineyard runs on three nodes with four processes on each node. Each node must unpack a data archive to its local disk exactly once before training starts, so only one process per node must run the unpack step.

Which environment variable should the training script check to decide whether a process runs the unpack step?
choices: `NODE_RANK`, and run the step when the value is 0
`RANK`, and run the step when the value is 0
`LOCAL_RANK`, and run the step when the value is 0
`WORLD_SIZE`, and run the step when the value is 12
explanation: Azure Machine Learning sets MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT, WORLD_SIZE, and NODE_RANK on each node, and RANK and LOCAL_RANK on each process. RANK is unique across the job, LOCAL_RANK is unique within a node, and NODE_RANK identifies the node, so per-node work usually runs where LOCAL_RANK is 0.
rationale: Incorrect: NODE_RANK identifies the node, so all four processes on the first node share NODE_RANK 0 and would all unpack the archive, while the other nodes would skip it.
Incorrect: RANK is the global rank across the whole job, so only one process in the entire job has RANK 0. The other two nodes would never unpack the archive. Use RANK 0 for once-per-job work.

Correct: LOCAL_RANK is the rank of the process within its node, from 0 to the number of processes on the node minus one. Exactly one process per node has LOCAL_RANK 0, so each node unpacks the archive once.
Incorrect: WORLD_SIZE is the total number of processes, 12 here, and it has the same value in every process. Checking it does not single out one process per node.

stem:
Wide World Importers trains a model with PyTorch DistributedDataParallel and the nccl backend on a cluster of Standard_NC96ads_A100_v4 nodes, which have four A100 GPUs each. A one-node job takes four hours. A four-node job takes almost three hours, and profiling shows that the GPUs wait for gradient synchronization between nodes.

You need to bring the four-node training time closer to linear scaling.

What should you do?
choices: Set process_count_per_instance to 8 on each node
Increase instance_count from four nodes to eight nodes
Change the communication backend from nccl to gloo
Move the job to a cluster of Standard_ND96asr_v4 nodes
explanation: Near-linear scaling across nodes needs fast GPU-to-GPU communication. InfiniBand provides it on RDMA-capable sizes with SR-IOV, typically the sizes with r in their names, and Azure Machine Learning clusters of these sizes come with the required drivers preinstalled. Sizes without InfiniBand communicate over Ethernet, which slows gradient synchronization. Learn's example pair, Standard_NC24rs_v3 and Standard_NC24s_v3, follows the same rule, but the NCv3 series was retired on September 30, 2025.
rationale: Incorrect: each node has four GPUs, so eight processes per node would oversubscribe them. The bottleneck is communication between nodes, which more processes would increase. Set process_count_per_instance to the number of GPUs per node.

Incorrect: more nodes add more gradient synchronization over the same network without InfiniBand, so the GPUs would wait even longer. Add nodes when the cross-node network is fast enough that scaling stays close to linear.

Incorrect: Learn recommends nccl for the best performance in GPU-based training. Moving to gloo gives up that backend and does not fix the slow network between the nodes, which is the real bottleneck.

Correct: Standard_ND96asr_v4 has r in its name and InfiniBand, so gradient synchronization between nodes gets low latency and high bandwidth. Standard_NC96ads_A100_v4 has no InfiniBand. Set process_count_per_instance to 8 for its eight GPUs.

stem:
You configure the command job for the shelf defect detection project with instance_count set to 3 and a pytorch distribution with process_count_per_instance set to 8.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: Each training process sees a WORLD_SIZE value of 24.
The command must start train.py with torch.distributed.launch so that each GPU gets its own process.
On the second node, the LOCAL_RANK values of the processes range from 8 to 15.
Gradient synchronization between the nodes can use InfiniBand.
explanation: For a pytorch distribution, Azure Machine Learning starts process_count_per_instance processes on each of the instance_count nodes and sets MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT, WORLD_SIZE, NODE_RANK, RANK, and LOCAL_RANK. RANK is global, LOCAL_RANK restarts at 0 on every node, and RDMA-capable sizes such as Standard_ND96asr_v4 add InfiniBand between nodes.
rationale: Yes: WORLD_SIZE is the total number of processes, three nodes times eight processes per node, which matches the 24 GPUs that the job uses.
No: Azure Machine Learning launches the processes itself when the job uses the pytorch distribution, so no launcher utility such as torch.distributed.launch is needed.
No: LOCAL_RANK is the rank within a node, so it ranges from 0 to 7 on every node. The values 8 to 15 on the second node are the global RANK values.
Yes: gpu-cluster uses Standard_ND96asr_v4, an RDMA-capable size with r in its name and InfiniBand support, so cross-node communication can use the low-latency InfiniBand network.

stem:
Lucerne Publishing builds a pipeline with the Azure Machine Learning Python SDK v2. The pipeline has a data preparation step, a training step named train_node, and a scoring step. The data preparation and scoring steps must run on a CPU cluster named cpu-cluster, and train_node must run on a GPU cluster named gpu-cluster.

What should you do?
choices: Set default_compute in the @pipeline decorator to cpu-cluster and set train_node.compute to gpu-cluster
Set default_compute in the @pipeline decorator to gpu-cluster and leave the compute of each step unset
Set default_compute in the @pipeline decorator to gpu-cluster and set train_node.compute to cpu-cluster
Submit train_node as a separate command job on gpu-cluster and pass its output to the pipeline
explanation: A pipeline-level default_compute applies to every step that does not set its own compute, and compute set on a step overrides the default for that step. This lets one pipeline run heavy training on GPU nodes and lighter steps on cheaper CPU nodes.
rationale: Correct: the default compute sends the preparation and scoring steps to cpu-cluster, and the compute set on train_node overrides the default, so only training runs on gpu-cluster.
Incorrect: with only a default of gpu-cluster, every step runs on the GPU cluster, including preparation and scoring. Use a single default when all steps need the same kind of compute.
Incorrect: this is the reverse of the requirement. The two light steps would use GPU nodes, and the training step would run on the CPU cluster.

Incorrect: a separate job breaks the pipeline into pieces that you must connect by hand, so the steps no longer run as one pipeline with tracked dependencies. Step-level compute keeps them in one pipeline.

stem:
Adventure Works Cycles runs a training pipeline several times a day while the team tunes the training step. The first step, fetch_rates, downloads exchange rates from a public URL; its inputs never change, but the data at the URL does. The other steps must keep reusing their earlier outputs when nothing in them changes.

You need to ensure that fetch_rates runs in every pipeline job.

What should you do?
choices: Set force_rerun to true in the settings of the pipeline job
Set is_deterministic to false in the fetch_rates component definition
Set continue_on_step_failure to false in the settings of the pipeline job
Set is_deterministic to true in the fetch_rates component definition
explanation: A pipeline step is reused when its component is deterministic, the pipeline does not force a rerun, and its code, environment, inputs, parameters, and settings are unchanged. is_deterministic defaults to true; set it to false for a component that loads data from an external source that can change, such as a URL.
rationale: Incorrect: force_rerun true reruns every step in the pipeline, so the other steps would stop reusing their outputs. Use it when the whole pipeline must run from scratch.

Correct: with is_deterministic false, the pipeline never reuses fetch_rates and always runs it, which picks up the new rates. Learn recommends this for components that load data from a URL that can change.
Incorrect: continue_on_step_failure decides whether the pipeline keeps running after a step fails. It has no effect on whether a step is reused.
Incorrect: true is already the default, so fetch_rates is reused when its inputs do not change, which is exactly the problem. Keep true for steps that give the same output for the same inputs.

stem:
Blue Yonder Airlines has a pipeline job in which a training step and a long data quality report step run in parallel after a preparation step. When the training step fails, the report step keeps running for another hour, which wastes compute because the results are discarded.

You need to ensure that a failure in any step stops the pipeline and cancels the steps that are still running.

Which setting should you add to the pipeline job YAML file?
explanation: The pipeline job YAML schema lists True as the default for continue_on_step_failure, so when a step fails, the steps that do not depend on it keep running. Setting it to false stops the whole pipeline at the first failure and cancels running steps. The schedule YAML schema lists False as its default, so set the value explicitly instead of relying on a default. Other settings control reuse (force_rerun), placement (default_compute), and the run time of a single step.
rationale: Incorrect: a timeout cancels the report step only after an hour, whether or not training fails, and it could also cut off healthy runs. It does not react to the failure of another step.
Incorrect: force_rerun controls whether steps can reuse outputs of earlier jobs, and false is already the default. It does not change what happens when a step fails.
Incorrect: serverless as the default compute changes where steps run, not how the pipeline reacts to a failed step, so the report step would still keep running.
Correct: with continue_on_step_failure false, the entire pipeline stops when one step fails, and steps that are still running, such as the report step, are canceled.

stem:
Alpine Ski House uses the Azure Machine Learning Python SDK v2. The prep.yml and train.yml files define two command components, and no pipeline YAML file exists. An MLClient object named ml_client is connected to the workspace. Steps whose inputs and code did not change must be able to reuse the outputs of earlier runs.

You need to build a pipeline in which the train component consumes the output of the prep component, run it once, and follow its progress.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: Decorate a function named sales_pipeline with `@pipeline(default_compute="cpu-cluster")` that calls `prep_node = prep(raw_data=raw)` and `train(training_data=prep_node.outputs.clean_data)`
explanation: With the SDK, you load components (from YAML, Python functions, or the workspace), compose them in a function decorated with @pipeline that wires outputs to inputs, call the function with the pipeline inputs to get a pipeline job, and submit it with ml_client.jobs.create_or_update().
rationale: Step 1: load_component() turns each component YAML file into a function that you can call inside a pipeline. The pipeline definition needs these functions.
Step 2: the @pipeline function wires the clean_data output of prep_node to the training_data input of train, which creates the dependency, and default_compute sets the compute for both steps.
Step 3: calling sales_pipeline with the raw input creates the pipeline job object. The pipeline-level input is bound to the latest version of the raw-sales data asset.
Step 4: create_or_update() submits the pipeline job under the sales-train experiment, and stream() follows its progress until it completes.
Incorrect: force_rerun True reruns every step, so no step reuses outputs of earlier runs, which breaks the reuse requirement. Use it only when everything must run from scratch.
Incorrect: az ml job create submits a pipeline that is defined in a YAML file, and no pipeline YAML file exists here. The pipeline is defined in Python and submitted with ml_client.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. submits the following pipeline job by using the Azure CLI:

```yaml
$schema: https://azuremlschemas.azureedge.net/latest/pipelineJob.schema.json
type: pipeline
settings:
  default_compute: azureml:cpu-cluster
inputs:
  raw_data:
    type: uri_folder
    path: azureml:raw-sales@latest
jobs:
  prep:
    type: command
    component: azureml:prep_sales@latest
    inputs:
      input_data: ${{parent.inputs.raw_data}}
  train:
    type: command
    component: azureml:train_sales@latest
    compute: azureml:gpu-cluster
    inputs:
      training_data: ${{parent.jobs.prep.outputs.clean_data}}
```

The prep_sales component does not set is_deterministic.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: The train step starts only after the prep step produces clean_data.
The train step runs on cpu-cluster because default_compute is set for the pipeline.
If the same pipeline is submitted again with unchanged inputs, components, and settings, the prep step can reuse its earlier output.
explanation: In a pipeline YAML file, ${{parent.inputs.<name>}} binds a step to a pipeline input and ${{parent.jobs.<step>.outputs.<name>}} binds it to the output of another step, which creates the execution order. Step-level compute overrides default_compute, and components are reused by default when nothing changed.
rationale: Yes: the training_data input is bound to the clean_data output of prep, so the pipeline service runs train only after prep has produced that output.
No: compute set on a step overrides the pipeline default for that step, so train runs on gpu-cluster. Steps without their own compute, such as prep, use cpu-cluster.
Yes: is_deterministic defaults to true and force_rerun defaults to false, so a step whose code, environment, inputs, and settings are unchanged is reused instead of run again.

stem:
Fabrikam Residences has a pipeline job named pipeline_job and a team in Seattle. The pipeline must run every Monday at 02:00 Pacific time.

Which trigger should you use in the JobSchedule object?
explanation: A schedule cron expression has the fields MINUTES HOURS DAYS MONTHS DAYS-OF-WEEK, where days of the week run from 0 (Sunday) to 6. Azure Machine Learning does not support DAYS and MONTHS values and treats them as *. Without time_zone, the schedule uses UTC.
rationale: Incorrect: the expression is right, but without time_zone the schedule uses UTC, so the pipeline would start at 02:00 UTC, which is the evening before in Seattle.
Incorrect: the first field is minutes and the second is hours, so 2 0 means 00:02, two minutes after midnight, instead of 02:00.
Correct: 0 2 means minute 0 of hour 2, and 1 in the days-of-week field means Monday. time_zone sets Pacific Standard Time so that 02:00 is Seattle time instead of UTC.
Incorrect: 1 in the DAYS field asks for the first day of the month, but DAYS values are not supported and are treated as *, so the pipeline would run every day at 02:00.

stem:
At Margie's Travel, User1 created a schedule that runs a retraining pipeline every night, and assigned a managed identity to the schedule. User1 later moved to another team, and an administrator removed the AzureML Data Scientist role from User1 on the workspace. Since then, every job that the schedule triggers fails. The schedule is enabled and its start time is in the past.

You need to make the scheduled jobs succeed again with the least change to the schedule configuration.

What should you do?
choices: Restore the job submission permissions of User1 on the workspace
Grant the managed identity of the schedule the Contributor role on the workspace
Disable the schedule and enable it again with az ml schedule enable
Set a new start_time on the schedule with az ml schedule update
explanation: A schedule submits jobs on behalf of its author. Even after a managed identity is assigned to the schedule, the author must keep the permissions to run jobs, or the triggered jobs fail. Schedules that do not trigger at all are usually disabled or have a start time in the future.
rationale: Correct: Learn states that the schedule author must retain job run permissions for the schedule to work, even with a managed identity assigned. Restoring them fixes the failures without changing the schedule.
Incorrect: the managed identity is already assigned, and it does not replace the permissions of the author, so the jobs keep failing. More rights on the identity would only widen its access.
Incorrect: disabling and enabling a schedule helps when it is disabled and does not trigger. Here it is enabled and triggers jobs, which then fail because of the missing author permissions.
Incorrect: a start time in the future stops a schedule from triggering, which is not the symptom. The jobs are triggered and fail, so changing start_time does not help.

stem:
You need to configure the nightly retraining pipeline and its schedule so that they meet the pipeline requirements.

Which three actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Create a JobSchedule with `CronTrigger(expression="30 1 * * *", time_zone="Eastern Standard Time")`
Use the `${{creation_context.trigger_time}}` expression in the output path of the pipeline job
Set is_deterministic to false in the definition of the ingest_supplier component
Use the `${{name}}` expression in the output path of the pipeline job in the schedule definition
Create a JobSchedule with `RecurrenceTrigger(frequency="day", interval=1, schedule=RecurrencePattern(hours=1, minutes=30))`
Set force_rerun to true in the settings of the pipeline job
explanation: A schedule pairs a pipeline job with a cron or recurrence trigger whose time zone defaults to UTC. Reuse is controlled per component with is_deterministic and for the whole pipeline with force_rerun. In schedules, ${{name}} resolves to the job name in output paths, and ${{creation_context.trigger_time}} resolves to the trigger time in string inputs.
rationale: Correct: 30 1 * * * fires at minute 30 of hour 1 every day, and time_zone sets Eastern Standard Time, so the pipeline runs at 01:30 head office time instead of UTC.
Incorrect: ${{creation_context.trigger_time}} is supported only for string type inputs of the pipeline job, not for output paths. It also gives the trigger time instead of the job name.
Correct: with is_deterministic false, ingest_supplier is never reused and always calls the supplier API, while the other steps keep the default reuse behavior.
Correct: ${{name}} resolves to the name of the triggered job and is supported in the outputs path of the pipeline job, so each run writes its report to a folder named after the job.
Incorrect: the recurrence pattern fires daily at 01:30, but without time_zone the schedule uses UTC, so the pipeline would not run at 01:30 in Eastern Standard Time.
Incorrect: force_rerun true reruns every step in each pipeline job, so prep, train, and evaluate would never reuse their earlier outputs, which breaks the reuse requirement.

A data scientist at Tailspin Toys has run 40 training jobs in an experiment named churn. The tracking URI is set to the workspace. The data scientist must load the parameters and the final metric values of every run in the experiment into a pandas DataFrame to compare them.

Which code should you use?
explanation: The Azure Machine Learning SDK v2 has no API to query logged metrics, so you query runs with MLflow. mlflow.search_runs() returns a pandas DataFrame by default, with one row per run and columns such as params.<name> and metrics.<name>, which hold the last logged value of each metric.
rationale: Incorrect: get_metric_history() returns every logged value of one metric for one run, given its run ID. Use it for a loss curve of a single run, not for a table of all runs.
Incorrect: search_experiments() returns experiments, not runs. Use it to find experiments by name, tag, or creation time before you search their runs.
Incorrect: get_run() returns a single Run object for one run ID, and churn is an experiment name, not a run ID. Use it to inspect the details of one known run.
Correct: search_runs() with experiment_names returns every run of churn as a DataFrame, with params.* and metrics.* columns that you can sort, filter, and compare.

stem:
A data scientist at Coho Winery uses MLflow connected to an Azure Machine Learning workspace. The data scientist needs a DataFrame of the runs in an experiment, ordered from the highest to the lowest logged accuracy.

Which code should you use?
explanation: When MLflow is connected to Azure Machine Learning, order_by supports run attributes, such as start_time and duration, but not expressions with metrics.*, params.*, or tags.*. To order by a metric, return the DataFrame and sort it with the pandas sort_values() method.
rationale: Incorrect: ordering by attributes.duration is supported, and Azure Machine Learning adds this attribute for convenience, but it orders the runs by how long they ran, not by accuracy.
Incorrect: this works in open-source MLflow, but Azure Machine Learning does not support order_by expressions that contain metrics.*, params.*, or tags.*. Use order_by only for attributes.
Correct: search_runs() returns a DataFrame with a metrics.accuracy column, and pandas sort_values() with ascending=False orders the runs from the highest to the lowest accuracy.
Incorrect: filter_string selects runs that match a condition, such as metrics.accuracy > 0.8, and DESC is not a valid comparison. Filtering does not order the results.

A team lead at Nod Publishers wants to review the training jobs that users canceled in the studio during the last week. The team lead queries the runs by using MLflow connected to the Azure Machine Learning workspace.

Which filter string should you use?
explanation: MLflow names run statuses differently from Azure Machine Learning. Not started, Queued, and Preparing jobs map to Scheduled, Running maps to Running, Completed maps to Finished, Failed maps to Failed, and Canceled maps to Killed. Values for attributes are always strings in quotes.
rationale: Incorrect: Canceled is the status name in Azure Machine Learning, but MLflow uses its own names when you filter runs. A filter on Canceled does not match the canceled jobs.
Correct: MLflow reports a job that a user canceled, or that the system terminated, with the status Killed, so this filter returns the canceled jobs.
Incorrect: Failed matches jobs that completed with errors. Use it to find broken runs; jobs that a user or the system canceled have a different status.
Incorrect: Finished is the MLflow name for jobs that Azure Machine Learning shows as Completed, which ended without errors. It does not include canceled jobs.

stem:
Two teams at Relecloud log runs to experiments named pricing-a and pricing-b. Each training script calls mlflow.log_param("model_type", ...) and mlflow.log_metric("auc", ...). You need the five runs with the highest auc across both experiments, considering only runs in which model_type is xgboost and auc is greater than 0.8.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```python
runs = mlflow.search_runs(
    [[1]]=["pricing-a", "pricing-b"],
    filter_string="[[2]] = 'xgboost' AND [[3]] > 0.8",
)
top5 = runs.[[4]]("metrics.auc", ascending=False).head(5)
```

targets.label: Box 1
why: Correct: experiment_names accepts a list of experiment names, so the search covers both pricing-a and pricing-b in one call.
Incorrect: experiment_ids also accepts a list, but it expects experiment IDs, and the code passes experiment names. Use it when you already have the IDs.
Incorrect: search_all_experiments is a boolean that searches every experiment in the workspace. It does not take a list, and it would include runs from unrelated experiments.

targets.label: Box 2
why: Incorrect: the attributes prefix covers run information such as status, user_id, start_time, and duration, not values that the script logs.
Correct: model_type is logged with log_param(), so it is filtered through the params prefix. For parameters, the supported operators are =, like, and !=.
Incorrect: the tags prefix filters values set as tags, such as tags.framework. model_type was logged as a parameter, so a tag filter finds no match.

targets.label: Box 3
why: Incorrect: auc is a metric, not a parameter, and parameter filters support only =, like, and !=, so a greater-than comparison would not apply.
Incorrect: attributes describe the run itself, such as its status or duration. Logged metrics are not attributes.
Correct: auc is logged with log_metric(), so it is filtered through the metrics prefix, which supports numeric comparisons such as greater than.

targets.label: Box 4
why: Incorrect: sort_index() orders the DataFrame by its row index instead of a column, so the runs would not be ranked by auc.
Correct: search_runs() returns a pandas DataFrame, and sort_values() orders it by the metrics.auc column. Azure Machine Learning does not support metrics in order_by, so sorting happens in pandas.

explanation: mlflow.search_runs() can search several experiments by name or ID and filters with params, metrics, tags, and attributes prefixes joined by AND (OR is not supported). Because order_by does not support metrics in Azure Machine Learning, sort the returned DataFrame with pandas.

Wingtip Toys runs a sweep job named sweep1 in an experiment named pricing. The sweep maximizes the metric auc and has completed. After completion, the SweepJob object was retrieved with ml_client.jobs.get() and stored in a variable named returned_sweep_job, and MLflow is connected to the workspace.

You need to identify the run ID of the best trial programmatically.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
choices: Search runs in the pricing experiment with `order_by=["metrics.auc DESC"]` and `max_results=1`
Search runs in the pricing experiment with `filter_string="tags.mlflow.parentRunId='sweep1'"`, sort the DataFrame by metrics.auc in descending order, and take the first run
explanation: A completed sweep job exposes the best trial in its best_child_run_id property, which Learn samples use to build the model path. Trials are child runs, so you can also query them through the mlflow.parentRunId tag and rank them by the primary metric yourself. AutoML jobs use a different tag, automl_best_child_run_id.
rationale: Incorrect: this reads a metric from the parent sweep run, not the ID of the best trial. The run ID is what the requirement asks for.
Incorrect: automl_best_child_run_id is the tag that Learn reads from the parent run of an AutoML job. For a sweep job, Learn exposes the best trial through the best_child_run_id property instead.
Incorrect: Azure Machine Learning does not support metrics.* in order_by, so this query does not rank runs by auc. Use order_by for attributes such as start_time.
Correct: the best_child_run_id property of a completed sweep job holds the run ID of the trial with the best primary metric, which you can use, for example, to register its model output.

Correct: trials of a sweep are child runs, and the job name of the sweep is its MLflow run ID, so the mlflow.parentRunId tag finds all trials. Sorting the DataFrame by metrics.auc in pandas and taking the first row gives the best trial.

A training script at Lamna Healthcare Company logs the metric loss once per epoch with mlflow.log_metric("loss", value, step=epoch). A data scientist must plot the complete loss curve of the run with the ID run1 to compare its convergence with other runs.

Which code should you use to retrieve the values?
explanation: Run objects and search_runs() results hold only the last logged value of each metric. To get every value of a metric that was logged several times, such as a loss curve, call get_metric_history() on an MlflowClient with the run ID and the metric name.
rationale: Correct: get_metric_history() returns every logged value of loss for run1, with its step and timestamp, which is what you need to plot the full curve.
Incorrect: the metrics dictionary of a run returns only the most recently logged value of each metric, so it gives the final loss, not the curve.
Incorrect: search_runs() also returns only the last logged value in the metrics.loss column. It suits comparing final values across many runs.
Incorrect: download_artifacts() downloads files logged as artifacts, such as images or models. Metrics are not artifacts, so there is no file named loss to download.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. ran a sweep job that tunes four hyperparameters. In Azure Machine Learning studio, a data scientist must see in a single view how the values of all four hyperparameters relate to the primary metric across the trials, and must be able to highlight a range of values on one axis.

Which visualization should you use?
explanation: The studio offers several views of a sweep: the metrics chart tracks the primary metric of each trial over time, the parallel coordinates chart relates every hyperparameter to the primary metric with interactive axes, and the 2D and 3D scatter charts relate two or three hyperparameters to the metric.
rationale: Incorrect: the metrics chart draws one line per trial with the primary metric at each logged interval. It shows how trials progress over time, not how hyperparameter values relate to the result.
Correct: the parallel coordinates chart has an axis per hyperparameter plus the metric, so all four appear in one view, and you can select and drag along an axis to highlight a range of values.
Incorrect: the two-dimensional scatter chart shows the correlation between two hyperparameters and the primary metric, so it cannot show all four hyperparameters in one view.
Incorrect: the three-dimensional scatter chart adds a third hyperparameter dimension, but it still covers only three of the four hyperparameters at a time.

stem:
A data scientist at City Power & Light wants to compare the parameters, metrics, and tags of three jobs and two registered models side by side in Azure Machine Learning studio. The jobs are separate command jobs, not trials of a sweep job.

What should you use?
choices: The parallel coordinates chart of a sweep job
The Responsible AI dashboard of one of the models
The compare feature for jobs and models (preview)
The Outputs + logs tab of each of the three jobs
explanation: Azure Machine Learning studio has a compare feature (preview) for jobs and models: after you enable it in the preview panel, you select the jobs and models and compare their parameters, metrics, and tags. Programmatic comparison uses mlflow.search_runs() across experiments.
rationale: Incorrect: the parallel coordinates chart compares the trials of a single sweep job. These jobs are separate command jobs, and the chart does not include registered models.
Incorrect: the Responsible AI dashboard assesses one model, for example with error analysis and fairness views. It does not compare the parameters and metrics of several jobs.
Correct: once you enable it in the preview panel, the compare feature shows the parameters, metrics, and tags of the jobs and models that you select side by side.
Incorrect: Outputs + logs shows the files and logs of one job, such as std_log.txt. Opening it for each job does not give a side-by-side comparison of parameters and metrics.
